speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: asked the Prime Minister in light of rapidly decreasing interest rates, whether MAS will proactively monitor our banks' housing loan rates to ensure that the downward revisions are timely and fair, so as to ease the financial burden of existing borrowers who are impacted by the COVID-19 situation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: asked the Prime Minister whether MAS will consider proactive measures that will help individuals/businesses to understand credit restructuring and credit counselling programmes since many will be facing financial difficulties due to the COVID-19 situation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As part of the Government's response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has been closely monitoring market developments and engaging the banks on a comprehensive range of relief measures for borrowers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS does not intervene directly in housing loan pricing as interest rates are determined by the market.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But MAS expects housing loan interest rates to be revised downwards in a fair manner where this is consistent with sustained trends in banks' cost of funding for such loans.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: How interest rates on housing loans fluctuate also depends on the loan terms that borrowers had chosen.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Currently, about a quarter of borrowers are on housing loans pegged to the Singapore Interbank Offered Rate (SIBOR) or Swap Offered Rate (SOR).

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These borrowers would already have seen interest rates for their loans come down over the past months, as falling interbank interest rates are passed on directly to these borrowers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Slightly over half of borrowers have housing loans pegged to board rates or linked to fixed deposit rates.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These rates generally change more slowly than SIBOR or SOR.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, borrowers are less adversely affected when market interest rates rise quickly, but also will benefit less when market interest rates fall quickly.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The remaining borrowers largely chose to be on fixed interest rates for the first two or three years of their loan.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These loans do not adjust to changes in market interest rates, but provide certainty and stability.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Notwithstanding these differences in interest structures, borrowers may refinance their housing loans to take advantage of lower interest rates.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, as a matter of practice, banks will charge a fee to borrowers wishing to refinance their housing loans when they are still within the lock-in period.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If there are borrowers who have difficulty paying the fee, they can put up an appeal and I am sure the banks will consider on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS also facilitates the refinancing of property loans should borrowers choose to do so, by not subjecting them to the total debt servicing ratio (TDSR), mortgage servicing ratio (MSR) and loan-to-value (LTV) limits for owner-occupied residential properties.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Kwek also asked whether MAS will help individuals and businesses understand credit restructuring and credit counselling programmes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our priority has been to prevent borrowers from encountering repayment difficulties.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS has been working with the financial industry to help individual and SME borrowers with a wide range of credit relief measures, without these impacting the borrower's credit record.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, individuals will be able to defer payments on their mortgage loans.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Likewise, SME borrowers may opt to defer principal repayment on their secured loans.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS has also worked with financial institutions and industry associations to promote awareness of the relief measures, and to help borrowers understand the costs and benefits of each relief measure so that they can make informed decisions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There will be borrowers who find the relief measures insufficient.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They will have to approach their banks to explore possible solutions, including restructuring their debts.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They may also approach the Credit Counselling Singapore, or CCS, for debt management advice and counselling.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: CCS has collaborated with banks to offer the customised debt management plan for such borrowers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To help borrowers on the debt management plans and who are affected by COVID-19, CCS will also assist with restructuring their repayment plans.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On an ongoing basis, MoneySense, Singapore's national financial education programme, actively educates the public on debt management options.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS will continue to work closely with the financial industry to support individuals and businesses through this crisis, and to educate borrowers on the relief measures available to them.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I am very encouraged to hear about the high percentage of loans that were deferred.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And so one suggestion I have heard from my resident is, can we get more jobs from SGUnited to help out with Credit Counselling Singapore as a temporary measure to help deal with the additional workload, because the more people we can help to restructure the debts, the better it will be for everybody including the banks in the long run.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: My residents hope that MAS continues to exercise vigilance on the rates.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: They pointed out to me a particular observation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The observation is that while SIBOR rates have gone down, rightfully so, the credit spreads have gone up recently at a very short time period.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: That means the SIBOR plus the bank spread.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: That does not seem to gel with the default rates that does not seem to be increasing rapidly.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, they do hope MAS can look at that, as well as the board rates movement very carefully.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On the first issue, I fully agree with Mr Henry Kwek.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think moving forward, the labour market is going to be quite soft, unemployment is likely to go up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On SIBOR rates, I do have to look into the details.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But if the Member is referring to mortgage rates, that could have a different market mechanism.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On the whole, from our observation, interest rates ought to be coming down and it really depends on the kind of loans that you have taken, whether it is a fixed rate, or whether it is a floating rate, and I think that will also affect.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I think that is what MAS will always encourage all banks to do.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Clerk will now proceed to read the orders of the day.
